title: For the Love of Reading
author: Karshner, Melinda
summary: Melinda Karshner, a veteran literacy specialist, argues that the science of reading and love of reading are not in conflict -- but that bloated basal readers may be in conflict with both, when teachers are not given room to supplement them with whole-class novels. Citing a podcast conversation with Timothy Shanahan, she draws the key distinction between instructional reading (what the basal is for) and the wider range of books students should read -- basals are what teachers teach with, not all that students should experience. Her own practice replaces most basal excerpts with complete, curriculum-aligned novels: Frindle at year's start (covering character change, point of view, figurative language, and author's purpose while hooking students on morphology), with the basal then used for its proper purpose -- targeted skill instruction and transfer checking. She advocates for cross-curricular integration (reading, social studies, science, and writing woven around module themes), arguing that knowledge-building drives reading comprehension and that this integration makes both teaching and student engagement stronger. The article's bottom line is a 'both/and' -- the basal does its instructional job, teachers do theirs -- and it is the space between, where teacher judgment about text selection lives, that often gets left out of instructional decisions.
points: Students gain virtually nothing from a single extracted chapter -- they cannot grasp character development or plot arc from isolated excerpts -- so replacing them with complete, curriculum-aligned novels is both pedagogically sounder and more engaging.

The basal curriculum's purpose, per Shanahan, is instructional reading: it is what teachers teach with, not all that students read; supplementing with novels is not departing from fidelity but fulfilling the curriculum's own intent.

Frindle works as a whole-class year-opener because it covers multiple focus skills in two weeks while hooking students on morphology and the living nature of language -- the novel earns the buy-in that makes subsequent basal work possible.

Cross-curricular integration -- reading landform poetry in social studies, informational text on plate tectonics in science, classroom magazines in writing -- deepens knowledge building and eliminates the time crunch that forces teachers to choose between subjects.

Approaching curriculum with integrity rather than strict fidelity means honoring scope, sequence, and skill targets while adjusting the text vehicle -- teacher professional judgment about which text best serves the instructional goal is essential, not optional.
quotes: The Science of Reading is not in Conflict with 'Fostering the Love of Reading' But... a bloated basal could be in conflict with both if teachers aren't given the space and supports to supplement.

In the basic program... it's shorter works... complete stories and things like that... but that isn't the only reading kids should be doing. That's instructional reading... they should be reading a much wider range of books than that.

When I approach any program, I approach it through the lens of integrity, not strict fidelity. That means honoring the scope and sequence, ensuring kids are taught the skills each day, and using the program materials in a way that best fits student needs.

Kids get very little from a single chapter pulled out of a book. You cannot fully grasp character development or plot from a short chapter and yet the line of questioning in most basals assumes you can. I find short excerpts from books simply aren't worth anyone's time.

Frindle is my jumping-off point to get students stoked about word study... The book hooks students immediately because it turns language into something alive and powerful. Suddenly words are not just memorized things in a dictionary... they are built, shaped, and changed by people.
With research continuing to highlight how knowledge building drives student success (especially in reading comprehension) it would be detrimental to students not to make shifts like this.

It's never either/or and teachers shouldn't have to feel like they are being pulled between just short passages or just whole novels. Students need a healthy mix of both. It's this both/and that often gets left out of instructional decisions.
